text: View \(z=e^{\pi i/4}\) as an eighth root of unity. Then the reciprocal sum is the complex conjugate of the first, so their product is its squared modulus; grouping \(k\) by the residues of \(k^2 \pmod 8\) collapses the sum to a simple multiple of \(z\).

Use the factorization
\[
x+y+xy=(x+1)(y+1)-1.
\]
Thus the equation becomes a factorization of a fixed positive integer; the inequalities \(0<y<x\) sharply restrict the ordered positive divisor pair \((y+1,x+1)\), leaving only the admissible pair.

Use positivity to select the unique positive real roots: \(y^3=1\) fixes \(y\), while the quadratic relation fixes \(x^2\). Then rewrite \(x^3\) as \(x\cdot x^2\), obtaining \(x\) from the positive square root of the known square.

Use the distributive law: scalar multiplication distributes over addition, and associativity lets the outer factor combine with the coefficient of \(y\) and with the constant term separately. Both sides are therefore the same affine-linear expression in \(y\).

Write \(a=2^x\) and \(b=2^y\). The logarithmic hypotheses become a linear system in \(x,y\); adding them isolates \(x+y=\log_2(ab)\), so the product is determined directly without solving for each factor.

Use congruence substitution: replace \(x\) in \(6x\equiv1\pmod m\) by its prescribed square residue, forcing \(m\) to divide a fixed integer. Factoring that integer and applying the two-digit bounds leaves only one possible divisor.

View the radical expression as a quadratic-formula root: isolate the square root and square to obtain its quadratic polynomial relation. Comparing that relation with the given quadratic then uniquely determines the constant term \(k\).

Cancel the common gcd in the congruence, then invert the remaining coefficient modulo the reduced modulus. Thus \(S\) is the positive part of a single arithmetic progression; its least two elements are consecutive terms, so their midpoint follows immediately from that residue class and period.

Use prime-power valuations: the gcd takes, for each prime, the smaller exponent occurring in \(20!\) and \(200000\). Since the latter has only \(2\)- and \(5\)-factors, Legendre’s formula for their multiplicities in the factorial reduces the claim to comparing two pairs of exponents.

Use the invariant that a quadratic’s coefficient sum equals its value at \(1\). Thus reinterpret \(a+b+c\) as \(f(1)\), then use the shifted description of \(f\) by choosing the input whose translate is \(1\).

Pass to reciprocals \(b_n=1/a_n\): the nonlinear recurrence becomes \(b_n=2b_{n-1}-b_{n-2}\), so \(b_n\) has vanishing second differences and is affine in \(n\). Thus \(a_n\) is the reciprocal of a linear rational expression, reducing the numerator–denominator claim to fraction normalization.

Factor the quadratic denominator into its two linear factors and clear denominators away from their roots. The resulting affine polynomial identity holds for all other real \(x\), so comparing coefficients uniquely determines the two partial-fraction coefficients.
Represent each summand as a difference of consecutive squares: \(2k+3=(k+2)^2-(k+1)^2\). The finite sum then telescopes, leaving only its boundary square terms.

Let \(n=\lfloor100r\rfloor\) and write \(100r=n+\theta\) with \(0\le\theta<1\). Then each summand is \(\left\lfloor(n+k+\theta)/100\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor(n+k)/100\right\rfloor\), so the fractional part disappears; the sum becomes a monotone block-counting function of the single integer \(n\), which the given total uniquely determines.

Use the generalized Chinese remainder theorem: the compatible congruences modulo \(8\) and \(6\) combine into a single residue class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(8,6)\). Thus the filtered numbers form one arithmetic progression, whose terms below the range bound can be summed directly.

Use the factorization
\[
(a+b)^7-a^7-b^7=7ab(a+b)(a^2+ab+b^2)^2.
\]
Since \(a,b,a+b\) are \(7\)-adic units, the required divisibility forces \(7^3\mid a^2+ab+b^2\); positivity and a small assumed value of \(a+b\) then bound this quadratic form below the least positive multiple of \(7^3\).

Factor the cyclic quartic as \((a+b+c)(a-b)(b-c)(a-c)\), then decompose \((a,b,c)\) into its mean direction and the orthogonal zero-sum plane. On that plane the Vandermonde product is a radial cubic times a triple-angle sine, so the problem reduces by homogeneity to balancing the mean magnitude against the centered radius.
Clear denominators by expressing both sums with a common denominator; then the product reduces to an elementary integer identity in the rational field.
Work in the multiplicative group modulo \(7\): the subgroup generated by \(2\) has odd order, whereas \(-1\) has order \(2\), creating the required order obstruction.

A positive integer has exactly three divisors precisely when its prime factorization is \(p^2\) for some prime \(p\): its divisors are \(1,p,p^2\). Thus \(S\) is naturally identified with primes whose squares lie below \(1000\), reducing the problem to a finite prime count under the square-root bound.

Because \(30\) is invertible modulo \(47\), multiply by its modular inverse to reduce the congruence to one residue class. All natural solutions differ by multiples of \(47\), so the canonical representative in \([0,47)\) is automatically the least.

Assuming the identity everywhere, comparing third iterates makes \(f\) commute with translation by \(1987\). Hence \(f\) induces an involution on the odd set of residue classes modulo \(1987\); a fixed residue class then forces two equal integer “height shifts” to combine into a single-step shift, creating a parity obstruction.

Use modular invertibility: since \(7\) is coprime to \(398\), multiplication by \(7\) permutes the residue classes modulo \(398\). Thus the residue class of \(1\) has a representative preimage, which can be chosen in the standard range below the modulus.

On positive reals, the functional equation makes \(x f(x)\) invariant under multiplicative rescaling: replacing \(x\) by \(xy\) divides \(f\) by exactly \(y\). Thus \(f(x)=C/x\) there, and the given value determines the constant.

Rewrite \(1\pm\sin(2x)=(\sin x\pm\cos x)^2\), turning the radical expression into \(2\min(|\sin x|,|\cos x|)\). The problem then reduces by the sign of \(\cos x\): one region is automatic, while the other compares the magnitudes of sine and cosine.

Complete the square after scaling: the quadratic equation becomes an equality fixing the square of the positive linear term \(3b+1\). Positivity removes the negative-square-root ambiguity, so rigidity of natural-number squares uniquely determines \(b\).

Reduce \(a\) by parity: write it as either \(2k\) or \(2k+1\). Squaring preserves this dichotomy modulo \(4\), since all nonconstant terms contain a factor of \(4\); thus the square’s residue depends only on whether \(a\) is even or odd.
Rewrite the range sum using the triangular-number identity \(\sum_{k<n} k = n(n-1)/2\); its residue modulo \(9\) then follows by reducing this product representation modulo \(9\).

View complex numbers in Cartesian form \(a+bi\): subtraction acts componentwise on real and imaginary parts. Here the two numbers have the same imaginary component, so it cancels, reducing the claim to a real-part subtraction.

Reparameterize by \(x=3y\): the fiber \(f^{-1}(\{7\})\) becomes a scaled copy of the roots of a monic quadratic. The desired sum is therefore a fixed scaling of the sum of those roots, which is determined immediately by Viète’s formula.
Use the difference-of-squares identity on \((x+1)(x-1)\); after multiplying by \(x\), its cubic term cancels the leading \(x^3\), reducing the hypothesis to a linear equation in \(x\).

Use the Euclidean algorithm: replacing a pair by the smaller number and the remainder preserves their common divisors, so repeated reduction turns the gcd computation into a much simpler terminal divisibility problem.

Use the order-preserving correspondence between nonnegative numbers and their squares: the square-root inequalities turn membership in \(S\) into lying in an ordinary bounded interval of natural numbers. Thus \(S\) is an integer interval, whose cardinality is determined by its endpoints.

Use the telescoping decomposition
\[
\frac1{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac1{k+1}-\frac1{k+2}.
\]
In the finite sum, consecutive reciprocal terms cancel, leaving only the two boundary terms; the remaining expression can then be rewritten in the desired rational form.

Use the prime-exponent representation of divisors: since \(36\) has two prime factors, every divisor corresponds uniquely to choosing bounded exponents for each. Thus the sum over \(S\) separates into a product of two finite geometric sums.

View the equivalence as the affine bijection \(t\mapsto 5t-12\), whose inverse is forced by solving that affine relation. Thus the hypothesis equates two affine expressions in \(x\), reducing the problem to a linear equation with a unique solution.

Parity forces one of \(a,b\) to be \(2\); positivity of the prime natural difference determines which one. The remaining hypotheses form a three-term prime constellation spaced by \(2\), and reduction modulo \(3\) forces one member to be the exceptional prime \(3\), rigidly determining the configuration.

View \((t-p)(t-q)\) as a quadratic centered at \((p+q)/2\). Equal values at two distinct inputs force those inputs to be reflections across this center, since the difference of the quadratic values factors into their difference times the difference from having equal midpoint.

View the summands as consecutive odd numbers: the sum of the first \(m\) odd numbers is \(m^2\). Thus the whole expression reduces to squaring the interval length and then reducing that square modulo \(7\).

Use elementary symmetric polynomials: the squared-difference hypothesis links \(xyz\) to the quadratic symmetric terms, so the cubic Newton identity factors the sum of cubes by the shifted sum \(x+y+z+6\); the cyclic-difference expression is automatically even, removing the remaining factor of \(2\).

Use the double-angle identity to replace each cosine square, then pair the resulting symmetric cosine sums via product-to-sum; the equation factors, up to a nonzero constant, into \(\cos x\,\cos(2x)\,\cos(3x)=0\). Thus the solution set is organized by the three arithmetic lattices of zeros of these cosine factors.
Reduce the base modulo \(5\): it is represented by \(-1\), whose powers alternate by exponent parity, so an even exponent fixes the residue.

Write \(11^k=(1+10)^k\); modulo \(100\), every binomial term of degree at least two vanishes, so each power reduces to its constant and linear terms. The whole sum therefore collapses to simple counts and an arithmetic-series sum.

View the finite family through AM–GM: fixing its product fixes the geometric mean, while the arithmetic mean cannot be smaller. The product condition also rules out zero factors, so the usual nonnegative AM–GM mechanism applies.
Rewrite the quadratic inequality as a product of two linear factors. A sign chart shows that such a product is nonpositive exactly between its two zeros, naturally producing a closed interval.

Natural-number subtraction truncates, so the sum is the triangular number \((100-x)(101-x)/2\). Divisibility by \(77\) does not determine \(x\) uniquely—indeed \(x=100\) makes the sum \(0\)—so the theorem is false as stated.
Substitute the fixed values and recognize the radicand as a perfect square of a nonnegative real; the principal square root then recovers that nonnegative base.
Use Euclidean division: write the dividend as a multiple of the divisor plus a smaller nonnegative remainder; modulo discards the multiple and keeps that remainder.

Use the symmetric identity \(x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2-2xy\): the hypotheses determine both elementary symmetric quantities, so they also determine the squared Euclidean norm. The square root then recovers its nonnegative magnitude.

View the hypothesis as an identity of quadratic polynomials: expand the factored side and compare the coefficients of \(x^2\), \(x\), and the constant term. The leading and constant coefficients directly determine the combinations \(ab\) and \(c\), so the target linear combination follows without solving for \(a\) and \(b\) separately.

View the hypothesis as a linear equation: repeated multiplication by \(2\) collapses to a single nonzero scalar multiple of \(x\). Since this scaling is injective over \(\mathbb R\), the equation uniquely determines \(x\).

Use the Euclidean algorithm: replacing a pair \((a,b)\) by \((b,\,a\bmod b)\) preserves their gcd, reducing the large inputs to a small terminal divisor; the remaining statement is then a simple arithmetic normalization.

Partition the integers into dyadic blocks \(2^j\le k<2^{j+1}\), where \(\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor=j\). Thus the sum is an explicitly computable, strictly increasing sequence formed from complete block contributions \(j2^j\) plus one linear partial-block term, so its value uniquely determines \(n\).
View the factorial modulo \(10\): its factors already contain both \(2\) and \(5\), hence a factor of \(10\). Consequently, every further multiplication preserves divisibility by \(10\).

View every factor as a monomial in \(x\): since \(x\neq0\), reciprocals of quotients can be inverted and all divisions by \(x\) canceled. The product then reduces by collecting scalar coefficients and adding the exponents of \(x\).

View \(a+b\) as twice the arithmetic mean of \(a\) and \(b\); convexity of \(x\mapsto x^4\), together with its homogeneity, controls the fourth power of this mean by the average of the individual fourth powers.
Rewrite the equation as \(c=-(2x^2+5x)\). Completing the square expresses this as a constant minus a nonnegative square, so its range has an attained maximum at the parabola’s vertex.

Use prime-exponent vectors: since \(30^4\) has three distinct prime factors, each divisor is determined by choosing an exponent for each prime from a fixed finite range. Thus the divisor sum of \(1\) becomes a product of three choice counts, after which the excluded trivial divisors are removed.

Use interval localization for the piecewise definition: standard bounds place \(\pi\) in the middle region \(0\le x<4\), where \(f\) is constant, so the negative and square-root branches are irrelevant.

View both hypotheses as equal-area rectangles. Positivity removes the ambiguity of truncated subtraction, and comparing the two area expressions yields a linear relation between rows and seats; combining this with the fixed product reduces the problem to a factorable quadratic with a unique admissible natural-number root.

Use the defining formula for \(f\): at the given input, the square-root radicand becomes a nonnegative perfect square, so the principal square root simplifies and the remaining affine expression is elementary.

View each hypothesis as a one-variable affine equation: isolate its variable by undoing the constant translation. Thus the two coordinates of the ordered pair are uniquely determined, and pair equality reduces to equality of the corresponding coordinates.

Rescale by \(x_n=5t_n\); the recurrence becomes the classical Lyness relation \(x_nx_{n-2}=x_{n-1}+1\), whose algebraic evolution is \(5\)-periodic. Thus the distant term reduces to one of the first five rational expressions, after which numerator and denominator are read in lowest terms.

View the equation as a linear equation in \(x\): combine the rational constants into a single nonzero coefficient, then cancel that coefficient (equivalently, multiply by its reciprocal) to isolate \(x\).

View \(p\) and \(q\) through function composition: \(q\) sends a nonzero input to its reciprocal-scaled value, and \(p\) then subtracts the square of that value from \(2\). Thus \(p(q(x))\) reduces to a simple rational expression for nonzero \(x\).

After canceling the common constant, the claim is the reciprocal AM–GM inequality: for positive \(x\), the gap in \(x+\frac1{2x}\) from its minimum can be rewritten as a square divided by a positive quantity.
Write \(n=7q+5\). Modulo \(7\), the multiple \(7q\) vanishes, and multiplication by \(5\) preserves congruence, so the remainder depends only on the given residue of \(n\).

Recognize the radicand as a perfect square, then factor its square root into distinct primes. Each divisor corresponds to choosing a subset of those prime factors, so the divisor sum factors as a product of terms \(1+p\).
The cross terms cancel, revealing the factorization \((xy-1)^2+(x+y)^2=(1+x^2)(1+y^2)\). This converts the problem into minimizing a product of two uniformly positive square-shifted factors.

Rewrite the absolute-value bound as a two-sided inequality; the preimage of that interval under the affine map \(a \mapsto 9+2a\) is again an interval, with strictness inherited from the original inequality.

Package \(x^2,y^2,z^2,w^2\) as residues of \(F(t)=\sum_a \frac{c_a}{t-a}\) at the odd squares. Since \(F(t)-1\) vanishes at four even squares, clearing denominators determines its numerator by those roots; comparing the next-to-leading coefficient recovers \(\sum c_a\).

Use sum–difference coordinates \(s=x+y\) and \(d=x-y\), so \(4xy=s^2-d^2\). Squaring the hypothesis makes \(d^2\) and \(s^2-d^2\) complementary nonnegative factors; their product is controlled by AM–GM (equivalently, completing the square), forcing the sum \(s\) to be sufficiently large.

View the recurrence through the finite state \((u_n,u_{n+1})\bmod 10\): its invertible update forces the digit sequence into a periodic Pisano cycle. Prefix sums then decompose into whole cycles of fixed total plus one bounded remainder, reducing the least-threshold claim to a finite comparison within a single cycle.

View \(q\) and \(e\) as complex conjugates: their product is the real norm-square \(a^2+b^2\). Multiplication by the purely imaginary \(d\) then scales this real quantity and rotates it onto the imaginary axis.

View the hypothesis as an identity of monic quadratic polynomials: comparing linear and constant coefficients yields a rigid algebraic system, with the nonzero assumptions allowing cancellation that uniquely determines both parameters.

Use modular exponentiation: reduce the base modulo \(5\), and exploit the short repeating cycle of its powers. Since exponents can be reduced according to that cycle, the large power’s remainder is determined without expanding it.

Rewrite \(|kx-1|=k|x-1/k|\), making the sum a weighted \(L^1\)-distance from \(x\) to the reciprocal points \(1/k\). This convex piecewise-linear function is minimized at a weighted median, where the total weights on the two sides balance.

Use Euclidean division: a natural number decomposes into a multiple of \(3\) plus a unique remainder smaller than \(3\). Thus the modulo operation discards the multiple-of-\(3\) part of \(71\), leaving its residue class representative.

Represent every admissible integer uniquely as \(19k+7\). The interval bounds then become bounds on \(k\), so the filtered set is in bijection with a consecutive integer interval whose size is obtained from its endpoints.

View \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) as distinct positive integers, so their increasing order statistics satisfy \(b_j\ge j\). Since the weights \(1/k^2\) decrease, the rearrangement principle minimizes the weighted sum by pairing the smallest values with the largest weights, reducing the comparison to the canonical sequence \(1,2,\dots,n\).

Split the sequence by parity: the odd-index recurrence advances by two while adding two, so \(f(n)-n\) is invariant along odd indices from the base case. Even indices are then determined from the preceding odd index by the other recurrence.

Because \(27\) is invertible modulo \(40\), the congruence determines a unique residue class for \(a\). Thus \(S\) is a positive arithmetic progression with common difference \(40\), so \(u\) and \(v\) are its first two terms.

View complex numbers as pairs of real and imaginary parts and use distributivity together with \(I^2=-1\). Here the two factors have matching component patterns, so the imaginary cross-terms combine while the real contributions cancel.

Take logarithms and rewrite the equation as a level-set condition for \(f(t)=\log t/2^t\). This function is unimodal, so the solutions lie on its two monotone branches; simple branch bounds then control their sum.

Complete the square: \(x^2+4x+4=(x+2)^2\). Thus membership in \(S\) becomes a bound on the square of the positive natural number \(x+2\), reducing the problem to counting the natural numbers in a short interval.

Double-count pairs \((S,s)\) where \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) and \(s\in S\): grouping by \(|S|=k\) gives the weighted binomial sum, while choosing the marked element first leaves every other element freely included or excluded.

Use the inverse-function identity: applying \(σ\) to \(σ^{-1}(33)\) gives \(33\). The stated cubic formula therefore turns the unknown inverse value into the unique real solution of a strictly increasing cubic equation.

Use unique prime factorization: rewrite the right-hand side as a product of powers of the distinct primes \(2\) and \(3\). Equality then forces the corresponding prime exponents to match, so the desired sum is determined by the total exponent count.

Translate each congruence into divisibility of a difference: admissible \(n\) must divide the gcd of those differences. Thus \(S\) is exactly the set of nontrivial divisors of one fixed integer, reducing the sum to its divisor structure.
Compare each radicand with neighboring perfect squares. Monotonicity of the square root then traps each irrational root between consecutive integers, which determines its floor and ceiling.

Use the identity \(|x+y|+|x-y|=2\max(|x|,|y|)\), which turns the constraint into the boundary of an axis-aligned square. The objective is a convex quadratic, so its maximum over that square is forced to an extreme point, reducing the problem to endpoint behavior.
Specialize the defining rule for \(s\) at the given positive arguments, reducing the claim to evaluating a sum of two natural-number powers.

View the divisibility condition as a linear congruence modulo \(6\): after removing the common factor \(2\), it selects a single residue class of \(n\) modulo \(3\). Thus the range splits into equal blocks of three consecutive integers, with exactly one admissible element per block.

Use the geometric-progression invariant \(u_1^3/u_3=a^2\), which eliminates the common ratio. Thus the given terms determine only the magnitude of the initial term, while the remaining ambiguity is exactly the symmetry \(a\leftrightarrow -a\).

Use distributivity to view the left side as a product of two linear factors. Expanding and collecting like powers of \(a\) yields a monic quadratic, with the linear and constant terms determined by the sum and product of the shifts.

Use the elementary symmetric quantities \(s=x+y\) and \(p=xy\): the hypotheses determine \(s+p\) and \(sp\), so positivity and integrality pin down the unordered pair \(\{s,p\}\). The target is then the symmetric invariant \(x^2+y^2=s^2-2p\).

View \(f\) as an affine function: its slope is the constant difference quotient between any two inputs. The two given neighboring values determine that slope and the intercept, so the value at any other point follows by affine extrapolation.

Use Vieta jumping: write \(a^2+b^2=k(ab+1)\) and regard it as a quadratic in \(a\). Its other integral root produces a smaller positive solution with the same quotient \(k\); infinite descent forces a terminal case, where the quadratic relation makes \(k\) a perfect square.

Use Viète’s formulas to encode \(a,b,c\) by their elementary symmetric sums. The key identity
\[
(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)-abc
\]
then determines the constant term of the monic cubic whose roots are the pairwise sums directly from the coefficients of \(f\).

View each alternating sum as a common alternating coefficient pattern applied to an arithmetic progression: the second progression is a fixed scalar multiple of the first. Linearity of finite sums preserves that proportionality, so the quotient is determined without evaluating either sum term by term.
Rearrange the inequality and complete the square: the difference between the right- and left-hand sides is a perfect square of an affine expression, so it is nonnegative.

Use prime-adic valuations: since \(15=3\cdot5\), \(15^n\mid942!\) exactly when \(n\) is bounded by both \(v_3(942!)\) and \(v_5(942!)\). Legendre’s floor-sum formula computes these valuations, with the scarcer factor \(5\) providing the obstruction and maximal exponent.

View \(f(x)-3\) as a scaled squared distance from the center \(x=2\). One known value fixes the scale \(a\), after which deviations from \(3\) at other inputs are transported by the ratio of their squared distances from the center.

View the three logarithmic differences as increments around the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\). Their sum telescopes to zero, so the three prescribed increments satisfy a single linear balance relation, which determines the unknown \(a\).

View \(n\) through its base-ten decomposition: equating the two expressions, canceling the shared digit terms, and factoring yields a product of \(a\) with a linear constraint on \(b\). Since \(a\) is a nonzero leading digit, the zero-product obstruction forces that constraint on \(b\).

View \(s\) as the integer lattice points satisfying \(|x+4|<9\). Translating by \(4\) turns this into a symmetric block of consecutive integers around \(0\), whose cardinality is determined by the radius.
Move everything to one side and view the result as an upward-opening quadratic in \(a\). Its negative discriminant means it never crosses the horizontal axis, so it remains positive everywhere.
Rewrite the place-value equation as a fixed ratio between the two digits; positivity and the single-digit bounds then leave only one possible digit pair.

View the nested expression as a finite continued fraction. Evaluate it from the innermost denominator outward; each layer is just rational addition followed by inversion, so the whole expression reduces to a single rational in lowest terms.

Use the prime-factorization divisor-count formula: write \(n=2^a3^b m\) with \(\gcd(m,6)=1\), so multiplying by \(2\) or \(3\) increments exactly one exponent while the divisor contribution from \(m\) remains fixed. Thus the two hypotheses constrain the same multiplicative factors, and multiplying by \(6\) increments both.

View \(t \mapsto t+2/t\) through its reciprocal-pair symmetry: after clearing the nonzero denominators, equality of the two values factors into a product involving \(x-y\) and a condition on \(xy\). Since \(x\ne y\), the first factor cannot explain the equality, so the reciprocal invariant must.

View the filtered set as the reduced residue system modulo \(8\): its elements pair by the fixed-point-free symmetry \(x \leftrightarrow 8-x\), so its cardinality is even. Since \(3^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 8\), powers of \(3\) modulo \(8\) depend only on the exponent’s parity.
Isolate the exponential term, then use that \(b \mapsto 4^b\) is strictly increasing—and hence injective—because the base is greater than \(1\).

Use the reciprocal symmetry: for any real root \(x\neq0\), divide by \(x^2\) and set \(t=x+x^{-1}\), so \(|t|\ge2\). The root condition becomes the linear constraint \(at+b=2-t^2\); thus Cauchy–Schwarz interprets \(a^2+b^2\) as a squared-distance minimization over lines indexed by the restricted parameter \(t\).

View the hypotheses as complementary decompositions: the \(5/8\) and \(3/8\) portions reconstruct \(b\), while the \(2/3\) and \(1/3\) portions reconstruct \(a\). Adding them gives a relation between the totals, and either original equation then forms a uniquely solvable linear system.

Reduce \(a\) to its residue class modulo \(3\). Squaring is compatible with this reduction, and the symmetry \(r \leftrightarrow -r\) collapses the three residue classes into just two square-residue types: the zero class and the nonzero classes.

Shift the distinct quadratic roots by \(1\): with \(u=a-1\) and \(v=b-1\), the target becomes \(1/u+1/v=(u+v)/(uv)\). Vieta’s formulas for the shifted quadratic determine this ratio directly; moreover \(1\) is not a root, so the reciprocals are well-defined.

Use logarithmic coordinates \(a=\log x\) and \(b=\log y\): positivity turns the product–power hypotheses into two linear equations in \(a,b\). The target \(\log(xy)=a+b\) is then obtained as a suitable linear combination of those equations.

Rewrite the factorial and powers as ordinary real constants, and use that \(\sqrt{9}\) is the nonnegative number whose square is \(9\). The expression then reduces by straightforward arithmetic normalization.
Use the change-of-base viewpoint: a logarithm compares exponents, so when both arguments are powers of the same positive base, the logarithm reduces to the ratio of their exponents.

Use prime-adic valuations: a reduced rational’s denominator is encoded by its negative valuations. If \(x\) and \(y\) had different denominator exponents at some prime, then \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) would have unequal negative valuations, so the more singular term could not be cancelled in their sum, contradicting integrality.

Factor the recurrence’s shift polynomial as \((E+1)(E^4-E^3+E^2-E+1)=E^5+1\). Thus the sequence is anti-periodic, \(x_{n+5}=-x_n\), hence \(10\)-periodic; the distant indices reduce to the initial recurrence window.

Represent \(10b+6\) as \(n^2\): its fixed final digit imposes a strong congruence restriction on \(n\) modulo \(10\), while \(1\le b\le9\) tightly bounds \(n\). Thus only a tiny set of square candidates can occur.

Take reciprocals and set \(k=(n+k)-n\): the ratio condition becomes an open interval of admissible integers \(k\), namely \(6n/7<k<7n/8\). Its length grows linearly with \(n\), so uniqueness is a lattice-point counting obstruction once the interval is too wide, while endpoint congruences handle the extremal case.

View the equation as an affine map in \(n\): remove the constant offset, then use that multiplication by the nonzero coefficient is injective on natural numbers, so the resulting value of \(n\) is uniquely determined.

For an affine function, the intercept cancels in differences: \(f(x)-f(y)=a(x-y)\). Thus every output change is proportional to the corresponding input displacement, so one known secant difference determines any other.

Use the difference-of-squares factorization over \(\mathbb C\): since \(I^2=-1\), the constant square can be represented as the negative square of a purely imaginary number. Thus the polynomial splits into conjugate linear factors, with the mixed terms canceling by symmetry.

Use modular stabilization: powers of \(5\) quickly become fixed modulo \(100\), since multiplying a stabilized residue by \(5\) changes it only by a multiple of \(100\). Thus every sufficiently large positive exponent has the same last two digits.

Decompose the level set \(f^{-1}(\{10\})\) along the two domains of the piecewise definition. The quadratic equation has no solution in its permitted region, while the affine branch is injective and contributes a single admissible point, so the finite-set sum reduces to that point.
Expand both compositions using the definitions of \(f\) and \(g\). Their quadratic terms coincide and cancel, so the commutation condition collapses to a linear equation in \(x\).

Use the Euclidean algorithm: the near-multiple relation between the two inputs reduces their gcd to a small common divisor. Then apply \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\gcd(a,b)=ab\), so the lcm is obtained by removing that shared factor from the product.

Set \(u=x\sin x>0\), turning the expression into \(9u+4/u\). The reciprocal-pair AM–GM bound gives its global minimum, while continuity of \(x\sin x\) on \((0,\pi)\) ensures the balancing value of \(u\) is attained.

Use the difference-of-squares factorization \(x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y)\). The first equation already gives one factor, while eliminating \(y\) from the two linear equations determines \(x\), and therefore the other factor \(x-y\).

Use compatibility of remainders under divisibility: since \(4\mid 8\), reducing a number modulo \(8\) and then modulo \(4\) preserves its modulo-\(4\) residue. Thus the given residue class modulo \(8\) determines the corresponding residue class modulo \(4\).
Work modulo \(20\): this simultaneously controls \(k^2 \bmod 10\) and the exponent class \(k \bmod 4\), which determines \(2^k \bmod 10\) through the four-term cycle of powers of \(2\).
Work modulo \(7\): discard the term containing a factor of \(7\), so the expression’s residue depends only on the constant part and its outer factor.

Exploit the period-four cycle of \(i^k\): split the weighted sum into consecutive four-term blocks.
